subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: State the typical spin-entry behaviour of an aeroplane that stalls while in a coordinated turn.
question_text: If an aeroplane stalls while descending in a co-ordinated left turn, it may enter
explanation: A stall entered during a coordinated turn tends to develop into an incipient spin in the same direction as the turn already in progress, because the inside (lower) wing is already closer to its critical angle of attack and yaw is already established in that direction.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The spin direction follows the existing yaw/roll of the turn (left), not the opposite direction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A spiral dive is an unstalled, accelerating condition, distinct from a spin, which begins at the stall.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A 'shallow left spiral' does not describe a post-stall autorotation; a stall departure in a turn typically develops into a spin, not a spiral.

learning_objective: Define manoeuvring speed (Va).
question_text: The manoeuvring speed for an aeroplane is the maximum

choices.label: A
choices.text: speed at which the aeroplane can be safely operated in smooth air.

choices.label: B
choices.text: speed at which full travel of the flight controls may be used without exceeding the design load factor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: speed at which the aeroplane may be flown with the flaps lowered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: safe speed at which the aeroplane should be operated.

explanation: Manoeuvring speed (Va) is the maximum speed at which full or abrupt flight control deflection can be applied without exceeding the aeroplane's design (structural) load factor limits.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That description more closely matches maximum structural cruising speed (Vno), not Va.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Flap-extended maximum speed is Vfe, a separate limit from Va.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This is too vague/general to be the specific definition of manoeuvring speed.

learning_objective: State the effect of airfoil icing on stalling speed.
question_text: If ice has accumulated on an aerofoil in flight, the stalling speed will
explanation: Ice accumulation disrupts airflow over the aerofoil and reduces the maximum coefficient of lift the wing can generate, which increases the stalling speed in all flight conditions, not just level flight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Ice significantly degrades aerodynamic performance; stalling speed does not remain unchanged.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Ice increases, not decreases, stalling speed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The effect is not limited to level flight; it applies across all flight conditions (turns, climbs, etc.).

learning_objective: State how indicated stalling speed varies with altitude.
question_text: The indicated stalling speed of an aeroplane

choices.label: A
choices.text: is higher when flying downwind than upwind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: does not change with change of altitude.

explanation: Indicated (as opposed to true) stalling speed depends on dynamic pressure/angle of attack at the stall, which the airspeed indicator senses directly; it does not change with altitude, even though true airspeed at the stall does.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Wind (a groundspeed effect) has no bearing on indicated airspeed at the stall.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: It is true airspeed, not indicated airspeed, that increases with altitude for a given stall.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Indicated stalling speed does not decrease with altitude; it stays essentially constant.

learning_objective: Compare stalling speed in a coordinated turn to stalling speed in straight-and-level flight.
question_text: The stalling speed of an aeroplane

choices.label: A
choices.text: is the same in a co-ordinated turn as in straight and level flight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is less in a co-ordinated turn than in straight and level flight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is greater in a co-ordinated turn than in straight and level flight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: increases in climbing turns, decreases in gliding turns.

explanation: A coordinated turn increases the load factor (wing loading) needed to maintain altitude, which raises the stalling speed above its straight-and-level value.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The increased load factor in a turn does change the stalling speed; it is not the same as level flight.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stalling speed increases, not decreases, in a coordinated turn.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The increase in stalling speed in a turn is due to load factor from bank angle, not specifically whether the turn is climbing or gliding.

learning_objective: State the risk of using low-octane fuel in a high-compression engine.
question_text: The use of low octane fuel in a high compression engine may result in

choices.label: A
choices.text: too lean a mixture for best operation.

explanation: Fuel with an octane rating lower than the engine requires is prone to uncontrolled, abnormal combustion (detonation) in a high-compression engine, which can damage engine components.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Mixture leanness is unrelated to fuel octane rating.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Carburettor icing is caused by temperature/humidity conditions in the induction system, not fuel octane rating.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Spark plug fouling is typically associated with overly rich mixtures or prolonged idling, not low octane fuel.

learning_objective: State the effect of a single magneto failure on a dual-ignition engine.
question_text: If one magneto should fail on an engine equipped with dual ignition

choices.label: A
choices.text: a slight loss of power would result.

choices.label: B
choices.text: there would be no effect on the engine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: half of the cylinders would not fire.

explanation: With dual ignition, each cylinder has two spark plugs fired by two independent magnetos; losing one magneto still leaves every cylinder firing (on the remaining magneto), just with slightly less complete/optimal combustion, producing a modest power loss rather than engine stoppage.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: There is a measurable, if modest, power reduction — it is not without effect.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The engine continues running on the remaining magneto; it does not stop.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Every cylinder still fires (via its remaining functioning plug/magneto circuit); it is not that half the cylinders go dead.

learning_objective: State the effect of applying carburettor heat on manifold pressure and mixture.
question_text: The use of carburettor heat will

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase manifold pressure and enrich the mixture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: increase manifold pressure and lean out the mixture.

choices.label: C
choices.text: decrease manifold pressure and enrich the mixture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: decrease manifold pressure and lean out the mixture.

explanation: Carburettor heat routes warmed, less dense air into the induction system; the lower density reduces manifold pressure, while the reduced air mass relative to the fuel metering enriches the fuel/air mixture.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Manifold pressure decreases, not increases, with carb heat applied.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The mixture becomes richer, not leaner, and manifold pressure decreases rather than increases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Manifold pressure does decrease, but the mixture becomes richer, not leaner.

learning_objective: State the temperature/humidity range associated with the most serious carburettor icing risk.
question_text: Under which conditions would the most serious carburettor icing be expected? Outside air temperature range of . . . . . and . . . . . humidity.
explanation: Per the carburettor-icing-probability guidance referenced in this study material, the most serious icing risk occurs with outside air temperatures roughly between -5°C and 15°C combined with high relative humidity, where venturi cooling readily brings moist air below freezing inside the carburettor.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Low humidity greatly reduces icing risk regardless of temperature range.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This colder band is associated with lower (not the most serious) icing probability in the referenced guidance, and pairs it with low rather than high humidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This colder band with high humidity is associated with a lower icing-probability zone than the -5°C to 15°C band in the referenced guidance.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: State that carburettor icing can occur at above-freezing outside air temperatures.
question_text: It is possible for carburettor icing to occur

choices.label: A
choices.text: in clear air with high relative humidity at above freezing temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: only when precipitation is present at freezing temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: only in cloud with high relative humidity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: only when water droplets are in suspension in the air.

explanation: The venturi effect in a carburettor cools the intake air well below the ambient outside air temperature, so icing can occur in clear air, at above-freezing OAT, provided relative humidity is high enough.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Carburettor icing does not require precipitation or freezing OAT; it can occur in dry, clear, above-freezing conditions given sufficient humidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Cloud is not a requirement; clear-air icing is a well-known carburettor icing hazard.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Visible water droplets in suspension are not required; invisible water vapour and the venturi cooling effect are sufficient.

question_text: Prolonged idling of an aircraft engine would most likely cause
explanation: Extended idling runs the engine with a rich mixture and relatively cool cylinder head temperatures, which promotes lead/carbon deposits on the spark plugs and fouls them.

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Pre-ignition is a high-power, high-temperature phenomenon, not associated with idling.

learning_objective: State the primary aerodynamic cause of ground effect.
question_text: Ground effect will enable an aeroplane to become airborne below normal flying speed primarily due to

choices.label: D
choices.text: an increase in wing tip vortices.

explanation: Close to the ground, the airflow pattern around the wing is altered, reducing induced drag (and downwash/wingtip vortex strength), which allows the wing to generate adequate lift at a lower airspeed than it otherwise would.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Ground effect improves (increases), not decreases, the lift/drag ratio.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Downwash is reduced, not increased, in ground effect.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Wingtip vortices are reduced, not increased, in ground effect — this is precisely why induced drag falls.

learning_objective: State the condition under which a 29.92 in. Hg altimeter setting indicates correct height above sea level.
question_text: The correct height above sea level is indicated on a pressure altimeter set to 29.92 in. Hg only when

choices.label: A
choices.text: the conditions of a standard atmosphere exist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: you are in the Standard Pressure Region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the barometric pressure is 29.92 in. Hg.

explanation: An altimeter set to 29.92 in. Hg only reads true height above sea level exactly when the full standard atmosphere model holds (standard sea-level pressure and standard lapse rate throughout the column of air) — real, non-standard atmospheric conditions cause the indicated altitude to diverge from true altitude.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A standard lapse rate alone is not sufficient; sea-level pressure must also be standard.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Flying in the Standard Pressure Region only means 29.92 is the required setting to use, not that it necessarily reads true altitude under non-standard conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Barometric pressure being 29.92 in. Hg at the surface alone does not guarantee a standard lapse rate aloft.

learning_objective: Calculate the altimeter reading error resulting from an incorrect Kollsman-window setting.
question_text: The altimeter setting is 29.70 in. Hg. If the pilot inadvertently sets 30.70 in. Hg on the altimeter subscale, the altimeter will read
explanation: Setting a higher pressure value (30.70) on the subscale than the correct value (29.70) — a 1.00 in. Hg error — causes the altimeter to over-read. Using the approximation of about 1,000 ft per 1.00 in. Hg, the altimeter will read approximately 1,000 ft too high.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The error direction is too high, not too low, because the incorrect setting is higher than the correct one.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 100 ft corresponds to a 0.10 in. Hg error, not the actual 1.00 in. Hg error in this scenario.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This combines the wrong magnitude (100 ft instead of 1,000 ft) with the wrong direction.

regulation_reference: Standard altimetry theory as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.
calculation_steps: Setting error = 30.70 - 29.70 = 1.00 in. Hg. Using ~1,000 ft per 1.00 in. Hg, and the setting being too high, the altimeter over-reads by approximately 1,000 ft.

learning_objective: State an early symptom of hypoxia.
question_text: A major early symptom of hypoxia is
explanation: Euphoria — an unwarranted sense of well-being and impaired judgment — is a classic, insidious early symptom of hypoxia, which is part of what makes hypoxia dangerous (the pilot often does not recognize their own impairment).

learning_objective: Describe the empty-field myopia effect on visual focus distance.
question_text: If you are looking at a featureless sky during hazy or dark conditions, your eyes will tend to focus at a point approximately . . . . . ft away.
explanation: With no visual reference points (a featureless sky, haze, or darkness), the eyes tend to relax to a short, near resting focus distance rather than focusing at infinity — a phenomenon known as empty-field myopia — which this study material identifies as roughly 3 to 5 feet.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This overstates the resting focus distance identified in the referenced material for this phenomenon.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This overstates the resting focus distance well beyond the figure given in the referenced material.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The eyes relax to a much shorter near-focus distance than several thousand feet; this option describes something closer to focusing at a distant/normal reference, which defeats the point of the illusion being tested.

learning_objective: State how the effect of alcohol changes with an increase in altitude.
question_text: The effects of one drink of alcohol at sea level will

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase with an increase in altitude.

choices.label: B
choices.text: decrease with an increase in altitude.

choices.label: C
choices.text: remain the same with an increase in altitude.

explanation: The mild hypoxia experienced at altitude compounds the impairing effects of alcohol, so a given dose of alcohol has a stronger effect at altitude than at sea level.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Altitude worsens, not lessens, alcohol's effects, due to compounding mild hypoxia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The effects do not stay constant; they intensify with altitude.

question_text: During an approach to land on an upsloping runway, the pilot may experience the illusion that the aeroplane is . . . . . than it actually is.
explanation: An upsloping runway tends to create the illusion that the aircraft is higher on the approach path than it actually is, which can lead a pilot to fly a lower-than-normal approach, risking landing short.

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The upslope illusion is not primarily an apparent-speed illusion; it is a perceived-height illusion.

question_text: When turning from downwind to into-wind at low altitude, a pilot may experience an illusion of
explanation: As groundspeed falls during the turn from downwind toward into-wind, a pilot can misperceive this as the turn being too slow/shallow, prompting an inappropriate skidding correction, with an accompanying false sense of decreasing airspeed — a known low-level turn hazard.

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The perceived airspeed change is a false sense of decrease (from falling groundspeed), not increase.

learning_objective: State the cause of wheelbarrowing on landing.
question_text: Wheelbarrowing on landing may result from a
explanation: An excessively high approach/touchdown speed keeps lift high and weight off the main wheels, causing the aircraft to balance and pivot excessively on the nosewheel — the wheelbarrowing effect.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A low approach speed tends toward the opposite problem (main-wheel-first, tail-low contact), not wheelbarrowing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Approach angle steepness is not the primary cause described here; excess speed is.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A strong crosswind creates its own handling hazards but is not the defining cause of wheelbarrowing.

regulation_reference: Standard landing technique/handling theory as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: State when wake turbulence from a departing aeroplane is most severe.
question_text: Wake turbulence caused by a departing aeroplane is most severe immediately
explanation: Wingtip vortices (the source of wake turbulence) begin forming once the wing is generating significant lift, which starts at rotation/liftoff — the wake is therefore most severe immediately following rotation, particularly near maximum-weight, low-speed, high-angle-of-attack conditions.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Power application alone (while still on the ground, pre-rotation) does not yet generate the lift-induced wingtip vortices that cause wake turbulence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Before rotation, the wing is not yet generating enough lift for strong wake vortices to form.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Above its flight path' does not describe the timing of wake generation relative to the takeoff roll/rotation being tested here.

regulation_reference: Standard wake turbulence theory as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: State the hazard when an approach into headwind encounters a sudden tailwind shear near the ground.
question_text: An aircraft flying an approach into a strong head wind encounters a sudden tailwind near the ground. The wind shear hazard to be expected is a sudden

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase in groundspeed and increase in lift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: decrease in groundspeed and loss of lift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: increase in airspeed and increase in lift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: decrease in airspeed and loss of lift.

explanation: Encountering a sudden tailwind after a headwind reduces the aircraft's relative airspeed abruptly, causing a corresponding loss of lift — a serious wind shear hazard, especially close to the ground where there is little altitude/speed margin to recover.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Groundspeed would actually increase, but that option pairs it incorrectly with an increase in lift, when the real hazard is a loss of lift from the airspeed decrease.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Groundspeed does increase (not decrease) when a tailwind is encountered; it is airspeed that drops.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Airspeed decreases, not increases, causing a loss (not increase) of lift.

regulation_reference: Standard wind shear theory as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: State the headings on which magnetic compass deceleration/acceleration errors are most pronounced.
question_text: Deceleration errors in the magnetic compass would be most pronounced on headings of
explanation: Magnetic compass acceleration/deceleration errors are most pronounced on east and west headings (the 'ANDS' rule — Accelerate North, Decelerate South — describes the opposite pair, north/south, for the related turning-error phenomenon on those headings, while accel/decel errors peak on east/west).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: North and south headings are where the acceleration/deceleration error is at a minimum, not maximum — they are, however, where turning errors are most pronounced.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This mixes a minimum-error heading (north) with a maximum-error heading (east), which does not correctly describe the pair of headings where the error peaks.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This mixes a minimum-error heading (south) with a maximum-error heading (west).

regulation_reference: Standard magnetic compass error theory as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: Calculate pressure altitude from aerodrome elevation and altimeter setting.
question_text: Aerodrome elevation 4,600 feet ASL. Altimeter Setting 29.52 in. Hg. Using the above information, what is the pressure altitude?
explanation: Pressure altitude equals field elevation adjusted by the difference between the standard setting (29.92 in. Hg) and the actual altimeter setting, at approximately 1,000 ft per 1.00 in. Hg. Since the actual setting (29.52) is lower than standard, pressure altitude is higher than the field elevation.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 4,640 ft does not correspond to applying the full pressure-altitude correction; it understates the adjustment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 4,560 ft applies the adjustment in the wrong direction (subtracting instead of adding).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 4,200 ft applies a far larger, incorrect adjustment in the wrong direction.

regulation_reference: Standard pressure-altitude calculation as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.
calculation_steps: Pressure difference from standard = 29.92 - 29.52 = 0.40 in. Hg. At ~1,000 ft per 1.00 in. Hg, correction = 0.40 x 1,000 = 400 ft. Pressure altitude = 4,600 + 400 = 5,000 ft.

subject: Aeronautics - General Knowledge
learning_objective: Estimate density altitude from pressure altitude and outside air temperature.
question_text: Pressure Altitude 4,500 ft. Temperature 20°C. Using the above information, what is the density altitude?
explanation: Density altitude rises above pressure altitude when the outside air temperature is warmer than the standard ISA temperature for that pressure altitude. The published density-altitude chart/table referenced by this exam gives approximately 6,100 ft for these conditions; an approximate rule-of-thumb calculation corroborates a similar figure.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 7,300 ft overstates the density-altitude increase for this ISA deviation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 5,100 ft understates the correction for a temperature this far above the ISA value at 4,500 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 4,500 ft would only be correct if the temperature exactly matched the standard ISA temperature at that pressure altitude, which it does not (ISA at 4,500 ft is approximately 6°C, well below the given 20°C).

regulation_reference: Standard density-altitude estimation as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool; precise value per the exam's referenced density-altitude chart/table, not reproduced here.
calculation_steps: Approximate ISA temperature at 4,500 ft = 15°C - (2°C x 4.5) = 6°C. ISA deviation = 20°C - 6°C = +14°C. Using the rule of thumb of approximately 120 ft of density-altitude increase per 1°C above ISA: 4,500 + (120 x 14) = 4,500 + 1,680 ≈ 6,180 ft, closely corroborating the published answer of approximately 6,100 ft.

learning_objective: Interpret the airspeed indicator's colour-coded arcs (Diagram #1).
question_text: Refer to the Appendix: AIRSPEED INDICATOR (DIAGRAM #1). The upper limit of the white arc on an airspeed indicator is the maximum
explanation: The white arc on an airspeed indicator marks the flap-operating speed range; its upper limit is the maximum flap extension speed (Vfe) — the highest speed at which flaps may be safely extended.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Maximum normal operating speed (Vno) is marked by the upper end of the green arc, not the white arc.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Manoeuvring speed (Va) varies with weight and is not marked as a fixed arc on the ASI.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Range speed' is not a standard ASI arc marking.

regulation_reference: Standard airspeed indicator markings.

learning_objective: Interpret a turn coordinator instrument depiction (Diagram #1).
question_text: Refer to the Appendix: TURN CO-ORDINATOR (DIAGRAM #1). The turn co-ordinator indicates that the aircraft is in a
explanation: The diagram shows the miniature aircraft banked with its right wing down (indicating a right turn) while the inclinometer ball is displaced toward the outside of the turn (away from the direction of bank) — the classic depiction of a skidding turn, here to the right.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The miniature aircraft symbol is banked right, not left, ruling out a left-turn answer.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The turn direction shown is right, not left.

learning_objective: Read head-wind and cross-wind components from a cross-wind component graph (Graph #2).
question_text: Refer to the Appendix: CROSS-WIND GRAPH #2. For a take-off on runway 31 with the wind from 270° at 20 kt, the aircraft would be subject to head wind and cross-wind components respectively of
explanation: Runway 31 has a magnetic heading of approximately 310°. The wind is from 270°, so the angle between the wind and the runway is 310° - 270° = 40°. Reading the cross-wind graph at a 20 kt total wind and a 40° angle off the runway gives approximately 15 kt head-wind component and 13 kt cross-wind component, matching trigonometric values of 20 x cos(40°) ≈ 15.3 kt and 20 x sin(40°) ≈ 12.9 kt.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 20 and 15 kt do not match either the graph reading or the trigonometric components for a 40° angle.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 15 and 20 kt reverses the head-wind and cross-wind values.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 13 and 15 kt reverses the head-wind and cross-wind values relative to the correct reading.

regulation_reference: Standard cross-wind component graph interpretation as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.
calculation_steps: Runway 31 magnetic heading ~= 310 degrees. Angle off runway = 310 - 270 = 40 degrees. From the Cross-Wind Graph #2 at wind speed 20 kt and 40 degrees: head-wind component ~15 kt, cross-wind component ~13 kt. Independently corroborated: 20 x cos(40 deg) = 15.3 kt; 20 x sin(40 deg) = 12.9 kt.
